question: Let $$A=\begin{bmatrix}2&-1&3\end{bmatrix}.$$ Obtain $A'$, determine the orders of $AA'$ and $A'A$, calculate both products, and establish from the resulting matrices that each product is symmetric.
explanation:
Transpose and Orders

The matrix $A$ is a row matrix of order $1\times3$. Therefore, its transpose is the column matrix $$A'=\begin{bmatrix}2\\-1\\3\end{bmatrix}$$ of order $3\times1$. Hence, $AA'$ is of order $1\times1$, while $A'A$ is of order $3\times3$.

Evaluation of $AA'$

We have $$AA'=\begin{bmatrix}2&-1&3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2\\-1\\3\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}4+1+9\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}14\end{bmatrix}$$ A matrix of order $1\times1$ is unchanged on taking its transpose. Therefore, $(AA')'=AA'$, and hence $AA'$ is symmetric.

Evaluation of $A'A$

Now, $$A'A=\begin{bmatrix}2\\-1\\3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2&-1&3\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}4&-2&6\\-2&1&-3\\6&-3&9\end{bmatrix}$$ Taking its transpose, $$(A'A)'=\begin{bmatrix}4&-2&6\\-2&1&-3\\6&-3&9\end{bmatrix}=A'A$$ Therefore, both $AA'$ and $A'A$ are symmetric matrices, although their orders are different.

options.B: $AA'=\begin{bmatrix}14\end{bmatrix}$ of order $1\times1$ and $A'A=\begin{bmatrix}4&-2&6\\-2&1&-3\\6&-3&9\end{bmatrix}$ of order $3\times3$; both are symmetric
